title: Server End-of-Life: Three Decisions
context: A customer database server is reaching end-of-support. It contains personal data and some records are still under a legal retention obligation. You lead its replacement and decommissioning.

n1.text: Before replacing the server, what must be verified first?

choices.text: The criticality, owner, and dependencies of the asset in the inventory
choices.why: Without an up-to-date inventory, you can neither plan the migration nor identify the affected data.

choices.text: The brand of the new server
choices.why: Hardware selection comes after analyzing requirements and dependencies.

choices.text: The number of cables in the rack
choices.why: Useful for physical relocation, but unrelated to data security.

n2.text: Some records are under a legal retention obligation. What do you decide?

choices.text: Retain the affected data for the legal duration before any erasure
choices.why: A legal hold suspends destruction, even if policy specifies a shorter lifecycle.

choices.text: Immediately wipe the entire disk to prevent any leak
choices.why: Erasing data under legal hold creates a compliance violation.

choices.text: Leave the disk in a cabinet without processing
choices.why: Storage without inventory or control remains an exposed shadow asset.

n3.text: For the rest of the disk, which disposal method is acceptable?

choices.text: Secure erasure or physical destruction, access revocation, and a certificate of destruction
choices.why: Proof of destruction and access revocation close the lifecycle.
Deleting file names does not make data unreadable: recovery remains possible.

choices.text: Resell the disk with service credentials still active
choices.why: Associated access must be revoked before any media leaves.

n4.outcome: You verified the inventory, respected legal retention, and produced proof of destruction with access revocation.

debrief: An end-of-life asset remains in the inventory until proof of its destruction.
Legal retention obligations override deletion policies.
Certified erasure, access revocation, and a certificate of destruction close the lifecycle.
